title: Plan your game: your client, your requirements, your storyboard and your data files
kind: a planning chapter: it earns AO1 marks
one: You choose a client and a topic, and you write numbered requirements that a test can check. Then you draw a storyboard of every form, a navigation map, and a table for each data file. You plan it all before you open Visual Studio 2019.

stages.title: Choose your client and your topic

screens.title: Find a client who has a real problem for your game to solve

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will have a client, a topic, and one paragraph that says what your client wants.
Every plan in this chapter goes into your portfolio. The marker gives marks for these plans (the AO1 marks) before you write any code.

words: One thing your game must do, written as one numbered sentence, such as R3.
Written so that a test can show it is true or false. "The game is fun" is not testable.
A drawing of every form in your game, with every button, box and menu named, and what each one does.
A drawing of how the forms link together: which form opens which, and how the player gets back.
A text file that your game reads from or writes to, such as `players.txt`.
One part of a line in a data file. In `players.txt`, the username is the first field.
blocks.intro: You do not need to learn these words now. Where you first meet each one in the chapter, it has a dotted line under it. Hover over it or tap it to see what it means.

blocks.p: Your client is a real person who wants your game. A teacher is a good client, because teachers know what pupils find tricky.
Ask a teacher one question: "What do pupils find tricky in your subject?" Their answer is your topic.
Choose a topic that is different from the Summit Ready topics in chapter 0. A game about knots, camping or the weather is not allowed.
Write what your client wants as one short paragraph, in their words if you can. Put the paragraph at the start of your portfolio.

box.title: An example to read: what the client for Summit Ready said

blocks.p: "Pupils going on their first expedition find the skills tricky: what to pack, reading the weather, grid references, timing a route, knots."
"They forget it all between the training evening and the hill. Can you make a game that makes them practise?"
Notice that the client names the problem, and names who has it. They do not design the game. You do that.
Your words must be your own. The Summit Ready plan in this chapter is there to show you the kind of thing to write. Never copy it into your portfolio.

stages.title: Write numbered requirements that a test can check

screens.title: Write requirements for moving between forms, typing in boxes, and what the game shows

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will have a numbered list of [[requirements|0]] for your own game.
A requirement is one thing your game must do. Number each one, R1, R2 and so on, because your tests and your evaluation point back to the numbers.

steps.see: Your browser shows that `requirements-template.docx` has downloaded. Open it in Word and save it in your portfolio folder.

blocks.p: Each requirement must be [[testable|1]]. A test must be able to show that the requirement is met, or that it is not.
For example, the requirement **The game is fun** is not testable. Two people can try it and give different answers.
The requirement **After 3 wrong tries in a row, the Log in button stays off for 30 seconds** is testable. You can try it and watch.
The mark scheme looks for 3 kinds of requirement: moving between forms, what the player types, and what the game shows and saves. Write some of each.

box.title: An example to read: Summit Ready's requirements for moving between forms

blocks.p: **R1.** The Log in form has a link, **Register a new player**, that opens the Register form. The Register form has a **Back to log in** button that goes back.
**R2.** A player who logs in sees the Welcome form, with their avatar, their last score, their best score and the Top 10.
**R3.** The **Start the expedition** button opens a map of 8 summits. Each summit opens its own game, in any order.
**R4.** Every game has a **Back to the map** button. It asks the player before leaving, because leaving scores nothing.
**R5.** The **Finish the expedition** button opens the Feedback form. Its **Save my score** button saves the score and goes back to the Welcome form.
**R6.** The Log in form has a File menu with Exit, and a Help menu with How to play and About Summit Ready.

box.title: An example to read: Summit Ready's requirements for what the player types

blocks.p: **R7.** The Register form refuses a username that is blank, or is not 3 to 12 characters long. It also refuses a username with anything but letters and numbers, or one that is already taken.
**R8.** The Register form refuses a password that is not 6 to 20 characters long. It also refuses a password with no letter, no number, or the bar character `|`.
**R9.** Each refused box shows a message under it that says what is wrong and how to fix it.
**R10.** A new player is saved as one line in `players.txt`, so the player can log in next time.
**R11.** After 3 wrong tries in a row, the Log in button stays off for 30 seconds and counts down.

box.title: An example to read: Summit Ready's requirements for what the game shows and saves

blocks.p: **R12.** Each game scores from 0 to 100 points, so the whole expedition scores up to 800 points.
**R13.** The Feedback form shows each game's score, with what went well and what went wrong, in full sentences.
**R14.** Each saved score is added as one line in `scores.txt`. The Welcome form shows the 10 best scores as the Top 10.
**R15.** Every game has a sound button that turns the sound on and off.
Your list will be different, because your game is different. Aim for at least 12 requirements, spread over the 3 kinds.
Each rule for a box is its own requirement, or part of one. In chapter 19, you test each rule with data that should pass and data that should be refused.
It is normal to add requirements later, when you think of something new. Number the new one at the end, and say when you added it.

stages.title: Draw a storyboard of every form, with the changes you made

screens.title: Draw every form, with every control named and what it does

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will have a storyboard page for each form in your game.
A [[storyboard|2]] shows every form before you build it. The marker wants plenty of detail, so show every button, box and menu, and what happens when the player uses each one.
Draw one page for each form. You can draw by hand and take a photo, or draw in Word with shapes.

steps.see: Your browser shows that `storyboard-template.docx` has downloaded. Open it in Word and save it in your portfolio folder.

blocks.p: Next to each button, box and menu, write its name, such as `btnLogIn`, and the words on it, such as **Log in**. Your code uses these names.
Beside each button, link and menu item, write what happens when the player clicks it, and which form opens.
Beside each box the player types into, write its rules and the message the player sees when a rule is broken.

box.title: An example to read: the storyboard notes for the Summit Ready Log in form

blocks.p: **Top:** a photo of the Mourne Mountains, the title **Summit Ready**, and one line that says what the game is.
**Menu:** File, with Exit. Help, with How to play and About Summit Ready. Each Help item shows a message box.
**txtUsername and txtPassword:** 2 boxes. The password box shows dots, not letters.
**btnLogIn, Log in:** if a box is blank, a red message says which box to fill in. If the username and password match a player, the Welcome form opens.
**btnLogIn, after 3 wrong tries in a row:** the button stays off for 30 seconds and counts down, such as **Try again in 27 seconds**.
**lnkRegister, Register a new player:** opens the Register form. When it closes, the Log in form shows again.
Draw your 4 game forms too, even before you know all of the code. You can add detail as you build them.

screens.title: Show the changes you made to your storyboard, and why

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know how to record each change to your storyboard, with the reason for it.
The top level of the mark scheme asks for a storyboard that shows the changes you made, and what you did about each one.
So keep your first drawings. When you change a form, draw the new version next to the old one, or write the change under it.
For each change, write 3 things: what was wrong, what you changed, and why the change is better.
Changes come from testing your game and from your client trying it. A change is a good thing to show. It is not a mistake to hide.

box.title: An example to read: real changes made to Summit Ready after a test run

blocks.p: **Pack the Rucksack.** What was wrong: the pictures covered the names of the items. What changed: the pictures are drawn smaller, at 64 pixels. Why: a player must read each name to choose.
**The map.** What was wrong: the title covered the score at the top of the form. What changed: the title is smaller. Why: the player must see the score at all times.
**Whiteout.** What was wrong: letters already tried looked the same as new ones. What changed: tried letters turn grey. Why: the player can see which letters are left.

**Listen Out.** What was wrong: clicking a picture before playing the sound did nothing, with no reason given. What changed: the first line now says **Play the sound first. You can play it 3 times.** Why: the player knows what to do first.

**The Log in form.** What was wrong: after a wrong password, the wrong password stayed in the box. What changed: the box is cleared and ready for the next try. Why: the player does not have to delete it.

stages.title: Draw how your forms link, and plan your data files

screens.title: Draw a navigation map of every form in your game

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will have a navigation map that shows how a player moves between your forms.
A [[navigation map|3]] is one drawing of every form as a box, with an arrow for each way to move between them.
In chapter 19 you write a test plan, which is a list of tests. The marker checks that it tests every arrow, so draw the map first.
Label each arrow with the button, link or menu item that moves the player, in bold, such as **Start the expedition**.

box.title: An example to read: the Summit Ready navigation map, written out arrow by arrow

blocks.p: Log in to Register, by **Register a new player**. Register back to Log in, by **Back to log in** or **Create my player**.
Log in to Welcome, by **Log in**. Welcome back to Log in, by **Log out** on the Game menu.
Welcome to the map, by **Start the expedition**. The map back to Welcome, by **Back to the welcome screen**.
The map to each of the 8 games, by clicking a summit. Each game back to the map, by **Back to the map**.
The map to Feedback, by **Finish the expedition**. Feedback back to Welcome, by **Save my score**.
In Summit Ready, every form goes back to the form that opened it. That keeps the map simple, and it is a good shape for your game too.

screens.title: Plan each data file as a table of fields

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will have a table for each data file your game reads or writes.
Your game keeps its players, its scores and its questions in [[data files|4]]. Each line of a data file is one thing, such as one player.
The bar `|` splits each line into [[fields|5]]. Your table lists the fields of each line, in order.

code.title: An example to read: one line of players.txt in Summit Ready
partLines: Field 1 is the username, field 2 is the password, field 3 is the avatar picture, and field 4 is the date the player joined.

blocks.p: For each data file, write its name, what one line holds, each field in order, and one real example line.

box.title: An example to read: the Summit Ready data-file table

blocks.p: `players.txt`: one line for each player. Fields: username, password, avatar picture, date joined.
`scores.txt`: one line for each saved expedition. Fields: username, total points, date and time.
`kit.txt`: one line for each item in Pack the Rucksack. Fields: picture, name, pack or leave, reason.
`knots.txt`: one line for each knot in Knot Pairs. Fields: picture, name, what the knot is for.
A username or a password may not hold the bar `|`. If it did, the game would split the line in the wrong place.
Write that rule into your requirements, so that you remember to test it in chapter 19.
Run each check below on your plan before you go on to chapter 2.

check.what: Each requirement has a number, and a test could show it is met.
check.how: Beside each requirement, write one line that says how you would test it. Rewrite any requirement that you cannot test.

check.what: A requirement such as "The game looks good".
check.how: Read each requirement. If no test could check it, rewrite it so that it names something a player can see or do.
check.fix: Change it to say exactly what must be on the screen, such as the words on a button.

check.what: Every form has a storyboard page, with every control named.
check.how: Count the forms on your navigation map, then count your storyboard pages. The 2 numbers match.

check.what: Every arrow on your navigation map names its button, link or menu item.
check.how: Look at each arrow. Each one has the exact words the player clicks, in bold.

check.what: Each data file has a table with every field in order and one example line.
check.how: Compare your example line with your table. Each field in the line matches the table.

blocks.p: Your portfolio now holds your client's words, your numbered requirements, your storyboard, your navigation map and your data-file tables.
Keep every first drawing of your storyboard. You add the changes beside them as you build and test your game.
